summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for configuring and monitoring an MPLS label switching router, the device that forwards packets by looking at short labels instead of full IP addresses. It covers the router's interfaces, label mappings and cross-connects.

plainLanguage.summary: Multiprotocol Label Switching lets routers forward packets by a short label instead of a full address. This RFC describes the SNMP tables that let a management system read and write the labels, interfaces and connections inside such a router, so that the same tools work across different vendors.

subtitle: The standard SNMP data model for configuring and monitoring a label switching router: interfaces, segments, cross-connects and label stacks.

tldr.problem: Operators need a vendor-neutral way to configure and monitor the labels, interfaces and connections inside an MPLS label switching router.
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB module defines SNMP tables for MPLS-capable interfaces, in-segments, out-segments, cross-connects and label stacks, plus performance tables with counters for each.
tldr.outcome: A label switched path through an LSR is set up by creating a cross-connect row and its in-segment and out-segment rows. Because the objects can change forwarding, the RFC says access must be protected, ideally with SNMPv3.

today: RFC 3813 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The module text says that the initial version of the module was published in RFC 3812, and that it works together with the shared definitions in RFC 3811.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular it describes managed objects for modeling a Multiprotocol Label Switching label switching router.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol, and the objects in this MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is a data model, not a protocol. It defines the names and types of the values a management system can read and write on a label switching router.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
A label switched path is modeled as a connection consisting of one or more incoming segments and or one or more outgoing segments at a label switching router. The association or interconnection of the in-segments and out-segments is accomplished by using a cross-connect. The terms connection and label switched path are used interchangeably where the meaning is clear from the context.

An in-segment is analogous to an MPLS label, and so is an out-segment. A cross-connect describes the conceptual connection between a set of in-segments and out-segments. Either set may be empty, so a cross-connect may connect only out-segments together, with no in-segments, in the case where a path originates on the router.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a label arriving, a decision, and a label leaving. The three tables in this MIB correspond to those three ideas: what comes in, what goes out, and how they are paired.

sections.title: Summary of the LSR MIB Module
sections.content:
Configuring paths through a label switching router involves enabling MPLS on MPLS-capable interfaces, configuring in-segments and out-segments, setting up the cross-connect table to associate segments or to indicate connection origination and termination, optionally specifying label stack actions, and optionally specifying segment traffic parameters.

The MIB objects that perform these actions consist of the following tables. The interface table, mplsInterfaceTable, is used for revealing the MPLS protocol on MPLS-capable interfaces. The in-segment and out-segment tables, mplsInSegmentTable and mplsOutSegmentTable, are used for configuring path segments at a router. The cross-connect table, mplsXCTable, is used to associate in and out segments together in order to form a cross-connect. The label stack table, mplsLabelStackTable, is used for specifying label stack operations.

Further, the in-segment and out-segment performance tables, mplsInSegmentPerfTable and mplsOutSegmentPerfTable, contain the objects necessary to measure the performance of paths, and mplsInterfacePerfTable has objects to measure MPLS performance on a per-interface basis. The objects for segments and cross-connects were derived from the Incoming Label Map and the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry as specified in the MPLS architecture document.
sections.plainLanguage: Six tables do the work: one for interfaces, two for the labels arriving and leaving, one for the pairing between them, one for label stacks, and three more for counters.

sections.title: In-Segments and Out-Segments
sections.content:
The in-segment table contains a description of the incoming MPLS segments at a router and their associated parameters, indexed by mplsInSegmentIndex. The index structure is specifically designed to handle many different MPLS implementations that manage their labels both in a distributed and a centralized manner. The table is designed to handle existing labels as well as future label strategies that may require labels longer than those defined in the MPLS architecture document. In those cases the object mplsInSegmentLabelPtr may be used to point at the first accessible object in a separate table that can represent the label because it is too long to fit in a single 32-bit value.

The out-segment table contains a description of the outgoing MPLS segments and their associated parameters. The in-segment performance table has objects to measure the performance of an incoming segment and is an augmentation to the in-segment table, and the out-segment performance table does the same for outgoing segments. High capacity counters are provided for objects that are likely to wrap around quickly on high-speed interfaces.

RowPointer is a textual convention used to identify a conceptual row in a MIB table by pointing at the first accessible object in that row. In this module the trafficParamPtr object from either the segment table should indicate the first accessible column in an entry in the tunnel resource table of the MPLS traffic engineering MIB, to indicate the traffic parameter settings for that segment if it represents a path used for a traffic engineering tunnel. The object may optionally point at an externally defined traffic parameter table, and a value of zeroDotZero indicates best-effort treatment. By giving two or more segments the same value, they can indicate resource sharing of things such as path queue space.
sections.plainLanguage: The two segment tables hold the labels arriving at the router and the labels it pushes, plus the traffic parameters for each. A pointer column links a segment to a shared traffic specification elsewhere in the MIB.

sections.title: The Cross-Connect Table
sections.content:
The cross-connect table specifies information for associating segments together in order to instruct the router to switch between the specified segments. It supports point-to-point, point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-point connections.

The operational status object indicates the packet forwarding state of a cross-connect entry. When it is down the specified entry will not forward packets, and when it is set to up it indicates that packets will be forwarded. The administrative status object indicates the forwarding state desired by the operator.

The label stack table specifies the label stack to be pushed onto a packet, beneath the top label. Entries to this table are referred to from the cross-connect table. The in-segment map table specifies the mapping from the in-segment index to the corresponding interface and label objects. Its purpose is to give the manager an alternative means of locating in-segments. It is useful, for example, when tracing paths from router to router by following the in-segment to the out-segment, retrieving the outgoing label and outgoing interface, and then interrogating this table at the next-hop router to continue the trace.
sections.plainLanguage: The cross-connect table is the actual switching instruction: which incoming label is joined to which outgoing label on which interface. Its status column says whether the router is forwarding on it.

sections.title: Counter Widths
sections.content:
64-bit counters are provided in this MIB module for high speed interfaces where the use of 32-bit counters might be impractical. The requirements on the use of 32-bit and 64-bit counters, copied from the Interfaces Group MIB, are as follows. For interfaces that operate at 20,000,000 bits per second or less, 32-bit byte and packet counters must be supported. For interfaces that operate faster than 20,000,000 bits per second and slower than 650,000,000 bits per second, 32-bit packet counters must be supported and 64-bit octet counters must be supported. For interfaces that operate at 650,000,000 bits per second or faster, 64-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters must be supported.

The interface group is also applied to MPLS. Each MPLS interface is represented by an entry in the interfaces table, with the sub-layer below the internetwork layer considered an interface. The value allocated for the MPLS interface type is 166. The octets and errors counters on that interface count labelled packets, and the count of received packets discarded during packet header validation includes packets with unrecognized label values.
sections.plainLanguage: A 32-bit counter wraps too quickly on a fast link, so the module also defines 64-bit versions and says which widths are mandatory at which link speeds.

sections.title: Example of Setting Up a Path
sections.content:
The RFC works through an example of manually creating a best-effort, unidirectional path. The path enters the router on MPLS interface A with ifIndex 12 and leaves on MPLS interface B with ifIndex 13, and no additional label stack is wanted beneath the top label on the outgoing labelled packets.

The first step is to create the cross-connect entry that associates the desired segments together. In the cross-connect table the entry has mplsXCIndex 0x02, mplsXCInSegmentIndex 0x00000015, mplsXCOutSegmentIndex 0x01, mplsXCLspId 0x0102 as a unique identifier, mplsXCLabelStackIndex 0x00 because only a single outgoing label is wanted, and a row status of createAndGo.

Next the in-segment and out-segment entries are created based on the cross-connect, although some agents may wish to create them automatically from the cross-connect. The in-segment entry has index 0x00000015, label 21 as the incoming label, a pop count of 1, interface 12 as the incoming interface, and the same createAndGo status. The out-segment entry has index 0x01, interface 13 as the outgoing interface, push top label set to true, top label 22 as the outgoing label, and the same createAndGo status.

The in-segment and out-segment cross-connect index objects are then automatically populated with the value 0x02 when these segments are referred to from the corresponding cross-connect entry. The RFC also notes that the proper use of createAndGo requires that all columns with no default value be specified for the SET to succeed, and that a subsequent retrieval on the conceptual row returns a different value such as active.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows the order: write the switch first, then the label that comes in and the label that goes out. The router fills in the back references itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This MIB module is potentially useful for monitoring of label switching routers, and it can also be used for configuration of certain objects. Anything that can be configured can be incorrectly configured, with potentially disastrous results.

A number of objects have a maximum access clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The in-segment, out-segment, cross-connect and performance tables collectively contain objects to provision MPLS interfaces, paths and their associated parameters on a router. Unauthorized access to objects in these tables could result in disruption of traffic on the network, and this is especially true if a path has been established. The use of stronger mechanisms such as SNMPv3 security should be considered where possible, and SNMPv3 view-based access control and user-based security must be used with any version 3 agent that implements this MIB module. Administrators should consider whether read access to these objects should be allowed.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive. The same tables collectively show the path network topology and its performance characteristics, so if an administrator does not want to reveal this information, these tables should be considered sensitive.

SNMP versions prior to version 3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, there is then no control over who on that network is allowed to read or change the objects in this MIB module. It is recommended that implementers consider the security features provided by the version 3 framework, including full support of its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to version 3 is not recommended; instead it is recommended to deploy version 3 with cryptographic security enabled, and then to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is configured to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: These tables can re-route live traffic, so writing to them needs the same care as changing a router's configuration. The RFC says to use the security features of version 3 of SNMP and not to leave the older versions running.

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE OF SECTION 7, SHORTENED TO THE ROWS THAT SHOW THE RELATIONSHIPS

data.title: Rows created for one path
data.code:
mplsXCTable:
   mplsXCIndex           = 0x02
   mplsXCInSegmentIndex  = 0x00000015
   mplsXCOutSegmentIndex = 0x01
   mplsXCLspId           = 0x0102
   mplsXCLabelStackIndex = 0x00
   mplsXCRowStatus       = createAndGo(4)

mplsInSegmentTable:
   mplsInSegmentIndex     = 0x00000015
   mplsInSegmentLabel     = 21
   mplsInSegmentNPop      = 1
   mplsInSegmentInterface = 12
   mplsInSegmentRowStatus = createAndGo(4)

mplsOutSegmentTable:
   mplsOutSegmentIndex        = 0x01
   mplsOutSegmentInterface    = 13
   mplsOutSegmentPushTopLabel = true(1)
   mplsOutSegmentTopLabel     = 22
   mplsOutSegmentRowStatus    = createAndGo(4)
